population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 18% of US adults (~47M) are currently on an incretin for any reason. Roughly 10% of adults are former users currently off the drug, so the off-drug population that has been on it is now more than half the size of the on-drug population. Growth came through the cash tier (subscription orals at $149–299), Medicare's Part D obesity demonstration (65+ roughly doubled from 9% to 16%), diabetes/cardiac/OSA-coded coverage, and about 1.2M low-dose 'quiet' subscribers, most without obesity. Income gradient: the top third leads despite higher obesity in the bottom third. The bottom third depends on Medicaid in the ~16 states that cover obesity, on diabetes codes, or on gray-market supply. An estimated 3M users (~6% of users) take some unapproved product, mostly mail-order Indian or Chinese generic semaglutide and 'research' retatrutide. Persistence is still poor: ~38% of weight-management starters remain on therapy at one year. 46% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once, usually at a coverage loss, a price step or a GI episode. Pediatric: 12–17 use rose modestly under specialist care. Under-12 off-label prescribing fell by about two-thirds after 11 states barred it. The upper-income skew in teen prescribing persists (~1.6×). US adult obesity is estimated at ~33.5%, down from 36.4%.

access.public_coverage: Medicare: the 2026 Bridge pilot rolled into CMS's Part D obesity demonstration (BALANCE) in January 2028. Medicare pays ~$245/month with a ~$50 copay where plans participate, so coverage is broad but not universal. The IRA negotiated price for semaglutide ($274) applies from 2027. Medicaid: ~16 states cover obesity at the federal rate. Several others dropped or never added coverage on budget grounds. Retatrutide is not yet in either programme's obesity coverage, pending its own price deal.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India $8–45/month and falling. Canada CAD 85–110. Chinese generics launched 2027 and are now the main low-cost exporter alongside India. Brazil and Mexico are generic markets. Generic semaglutide is available in ~170 countries. US exclusivity is unchanged (~2031–32). FDA has blocked bulk importation and warns against personal importation without seizing at scale.
access.note: The price path stalled. The scheduled cash step-down from ~$350 to $245 was paused in mid-2027 when Lilly and Novo invoked capacity provisions; HHS accepted in exchange for onshore manufacturing commitments. Cash prices: $299–349/month for injectable semaglutide and tirzepatide, $149 for oral starter doses rising to $249–299 at maintenance. Retatrutide lists at ~$1,399 with LillyDirect cash at ~$799, allocated by supply. Employer coverage for weight management fell from 60% to 44% (FICTIONAL, BGH-style survey). Most remaining plans require a T2D, established CVD, OSA, MASH or CKD code, and payers now audit for 'coding drift'. The 503A/503B compounding exclusion is final. Demand that compounders used to serve has moved to mail-order foreign generics.

on_market_classes: GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Dec 2027, launched Feb 2028)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved early 2027 for obesity; modest uptake after losing to tirzepatide head-to-head)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill, 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'quiet' / craving-and-calm low-dose oral plans sold through telehealth as wellness, mostly to adults with BMI under 30; no indication or trial supports them
alcohol reduction: phase 3 AUD trials of semaglutide still enrolling; no approval; widely prescribed off-label to heavy drinkers with comorbid overweight
microdosing for 'metabolic health' among non-obese affluent adults
nicotine and gambling craving: anecdotal and observational only
pre-bariatric and in place of bariatric surgery: retatrutide as a surgical alternative, ahead of any formal guideline
drugs.pipeline_note: No new indication this step. Semaglutide Alzheimer's (evoke) failed in 2025. AUD phase 3 readouts are expected 2029. Tirzepatide's CV label filing is still under review. Retatrutide label: ~28.7% mean loss at 80 weeks, ~30% in BMI≥35. It carries the dysesthesia and discontinuation data from phase 3, and postmarketing has produced nothing beyond them. Amycretin phase 3 is ongoing. MariTide monthly injectable phase 3 reads out in 2029. Bimagrumab-style muscle-preserving adjuncts are in phase 2/3 and heavily anticipated given the muscle ideal. Global incretin market ~$115B in 2028. US revenue grows on volume at flat prices; ex-US revenue is eroding to generics.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation. It is more frequent during retatrutide escalation, and slower titration schedules are now standard.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; severe-gastroparesis language retained across the class.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss. Absolute numbers are rising with retatrutide's larger and faster losses, consistent with known risk.
No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs; absolute risk low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; mass-tort litigation ongoing, no verdicts establishing causation.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Roughly 25–40% of weight lost is lean mass depending on population. Absolute lean loss is larger with ~29% total loss, which concentrates concern in older Medicare users. The 2026 bone-density signal is unresolved.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. Professional societies (2027) recommend resistance training and protein targets for older users. Industry is pursuing muscle-preserving adjuncts.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohort studies still conflict; no new data resolving direction.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: EMA 'very rare' label for semaglutide; still no US class label.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association found by EMA, MHRA or the 2025 systematic review. Nothing new.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Uncontrolled patient surveys (2027) find 10–15% of users reporting reduced enjoyment beyond food, but no RCT has measured it. It is the same effect telehealth 'quiet' plans now sell as calm and focus.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FDA untitled letters and FTC actions target promotional claims of calm and focus as unapproved uses, not the effect itself.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Large regain after stopping is consistent across trials. Real-world claims data still show smaller regain. Cycling (46% of ever-users) makes this a population-level phenomenon.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None. It keeps underwriting chronic-therapy pricing and payers' reluctance.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Concern grows with higher-efficacy agents and low intake, but no new signal beyond the 2026 review.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None formal; dietitian referral recommended in society guidance.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects in adolescents who may take these for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exists. There is still no cycling or adolescent-decade data, and the 2026 teen cohort is now mid-adolescence.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on retatrutide and orforglipron. Several state laws now require registry enrolment for under-18 prescribing.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Compounded supply has ended legally. Harm reports shifted to mail-order foreign generics and 'research-grade' retatrutide vials: dosing errors, mislabelled concentrations, unsterile reconstitution.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: 503A/503B exclusion final (2027). CBP and FDA import alerts, enforced selectively.

food_and_beverage.state: GLP-1 households are ~30% of US households. Cumulative US volume decline since 2025 is ~4–6% in snacks and confectionery and ~3% in sugary drinks; total calorie demand is down ~2%. Protein, fibre and portion-tiered SKUs are standard. Marketing has split in two: 'right-sized' lines for on-drug households, and frank indulgence ('eat like you mean it') aimed at people who want to be seen hungry. Mid-tier snack brands are being consolidated. No major company has failed.

alcohol.state: US spirits and beer volumes keep falling (~3–4%/yr). Off-label AUD prescribing and 'quiet' plans, which users report dull the wish to drink, add to Gen Z moderation. Premium single-serve and non-alcoholic lines grow but do not offset the loss of heavy drinkers. Layoffs at mid-size distillers; Diageo and Brown-Forman are cutting brands.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat. Casual-dining check sizes are down and mid-tier chains are squeezed. Small-plate and half-portion menus are standard, and the high end does well with 'appetite' tasting menus and steakhouses for diners performing hunger. Fast food is holding on value and on lower-income, less-medicated customers.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking, with store closures at Torrid-type chains. Mainstream brands have absorbed the smaller-size wave. Growth is in 'athletic' and muscle-fit cuts, tailoring and alterations, and size-fluid stretch lines for people who cycle.

fitness.state: Strength gyms, coaching and body-composition scanning are growing. Muscle has moved from preservation to display. Protein and creatine supplements are booming. A gray market in peptides and testosterone is growing in the muscle-ideal subculture.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is at 44%, and what remains is mostly coded to diabetes, cardiac, OSA or liver diagnoses with stiff prior authorisation and coding audits. Pharmacy trend is still high (~9–10%) because coded and Medicare volume keeps rising at flat prices. Some carriers sell standalone 'metabolic riders'. Two tiers are now formalised: coded patients pay copays, obesity-only patients pay cash.

pharma.state: Lilly holds ~60% of the US incretin market, helped by its orals and retatrutide. Novo is restructuring, defending semaglutide on price ex-US and losing share at home. US revenue grows on volume because prices are flat. Retatrutide is supply-allocated. Ex-US branded revenue is eroding to Indian and Chinese generics. Advertising restrictions have cut promotional spend and shifted it to physician detailing and direct-pay platforms.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A thin body now reads by default as medicated, so it no longer carries much status. Visible muscle, a big appetite and claimed 'unmedicated vitality' read as scarce, because they suggest time, money for trainers and food, and not needing the drug. Many people who display muscle are also on a pen; the claim is policed loosely and argued about constantly.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Partly inverted. Thinness no longer separates the top third from the middle, since cash-pay orals put it within reach of the middle class at $149–299/month. Muscle now does that work. The affluent quietly combine retatrutide with coaching, or perform being unmedicated. The bottom third has the highest obesity, the least coverage and the most gray-market use. Being heavy is still stigmatised, and is increasingly read as not being able to afford the pen rather than as a lack of willpower.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Mixed tables are normal: on-drug diners eat small plates beside performative eaters. Finishing a full plate in public has become a social signal. Some on-drug people eat bigger in public to look unmedicated. Family dinners where one partner is coded and covered and the other pays cash or abstains are a common domestic arrangement.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating profiles commonly state 'unmedicated' or 'on reta' as an identity marker. Libido and connection complaints from on-drug partners are discussed openly in advice columns. Couples where only one partner is on the drug report mismatched appetites in food, drink and sex. None of this is quantified.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has split into two meanings. As craving, it is something to buy relief from: food noise, the evening drink, scrolling. As hunger, it is a sign of being alive and a status display. The same culture treats one as a defect and the other as vitality.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Uncontrolled 2027 surveys put reduced non-food enjoyment at 10–15% of users. Among ~1.2M 'quiet' subscribers it is the stated reason for use rather than a complaint. There are still no RCT measurements, and the effect remains 'emerging' in the ledger.
interior_life.framing: Feature, sold under names like 'quiet' and 'steady': calm, focus, freedom from craving. Medically it is still an unquantified side effect. Telehealth firms market it while avoiding explicit claims, and regulators police the marketing but not the use.
interior_life.effect_on_work: In sales, finance, call centres and tech, managers call on-drug staff 'unflappable'. Some workers say they start the drug to stop stress-snacking and doom-scrolling at their desks. A minority report lost ambition and quit side projects. Employers do not encourage use; most now drop coverage while informally liking the results.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Critics argue about 'flat' work. Some musicians and comedians lower or stop their dose before tours and say so publicly. 'Unmedicated' is a selling point in live music and stand-up. Intense-reward hobbies grow among users seeking to feel more: sour and spicy foods, extreme sports, loud venues.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Users report reduced desire and the feeling of being steady but distant. Partners describe the change as kinder and less present at once. Some couples time dose reductions around holidays. Not quantified.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: No measurable effect on turnout or polarisation. The drug has become a political object. 'Unmedicated' is a shared identity for MAHA-aligned populists and crunchy-left wellness culture, and both sides frame the 'quiet' market as pacification. Commentators speculate about calmer electorates without evidence.

state.regulatory_posture: Split. Federal regulators are pro-speed on approvals, with retatrutide approved under a priority voucher, while FDA, FTC and the states tightened promotion, telehealth and minors' access. The MAHA-led HHS treats incretin advertising and 'wellness' use as a problem even as it brokers access deals.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No mandate. Medicare's Part D obesity demonstration (BALANCE) at ~$245 with a ~$50 copay where plans participate. Medicaid obesity coverage in ~16 states. The federal cash-price step-down was paused at $299–349. No subsidy for retatrutide.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Telehealth weight-management starts require a synchronous visit and documented BMI ≥27 with a comorbidity, or ≥30. Several states cap first prescriptions at a 90-day supply pending an in-person follow-up. Payer coding audits target 'drift' toward cardiac and OSA codes. 11 states bar under-12 prescribing and require a specialist, parental consent and registry enrolment for 12–17. There is no adherence surveillance beyond claims.
state.workforce_or_military: The Pentagon allows GLP-1 use to meet body-composition standards only through military treatment facilities. Recruits who used the drugs need a documented stable period before accession. Civilian employers make no requirements.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: The price gap is now a fixed political fact: Toronto ~CAD 100 against Dayton $299+. China joined India as a generic exporter in 2027. The US blocks bulk importation and tolerates small parcels. Lilly and Novo traded the paused price cuts for onshore fill-finish capacity and tariff relief. Retatrutide is US-first and supply-constrained.

events.event: Employer survey: share of large employers covering weight-management GLP-1s falls to ~50%; several Fortune 100 firms limit coverage to diabetes, established cardiovascular disease and sleep-apnoea codes
Lilly and Novo pause the scheduled cash-price step-down to $245, citing capacity and demand; HHS accepts in exchange for onshore manufacturing pledges, leaving cash injectables at $299–349
Telehealth 'quiet' subscriptions offering low-dose oral GLP-1s for calm, focus and craving pass one million subscribers; FDA issues untitled letters over unapproved-use claims
FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide, a triple agonist with ~29% mean weight loss; Feb 2028 launch at ~$1,399 list with supply allocation and waitlists; bariatric referrals dip

FDA and FTC restrict broadcast and influencer incretin advertising and require synchronous telehealth visits with BMI documentation; by mid-year 11 states bar under-12 prescribing and add registries for teens
Gallup: 18.1% of US adults now on an incretin; for the first time more adults name 'muscular' than 'thin' as the body that signals health and discipline

open_tensions: The two tiers have hardened. Diagnosis codes get a copay, obesity alone gets a stalled cash price or a mailed foreign generic, and retatrutide's surgical-grade loss goes first to those who can pay $799 a month or get onto an allocation list.

Calm is being sold as a product while the same effect is still logged as an unquantified side effect. Regulators have curbed the advertising but not the use, and no trial is designed to tell whether 'quiet' is relief or loss.

The muscle ideal is rising at the same moment the most effective drug strips the most lean mass. That pushes demand toward unapproved peptides, testosterone and muscle adjuncts that are still in trials.

The cycling population (46% of ever-users) and the 2026 teen cohort are growing up with no long-horizon data. New state restrictions limit new child starts but say nothing about the teenagers already on the drug.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: In 2028 the status body is muscled, hungry and proudly unmedicated, and you pay to stay calm
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028 nearly one American adult in five is on an incretin drug, about 18 percent, and another one in ten has taken one and stopped. The drugs have become ordinary the way statins are ordinary, except that statins are covered. Employers kept retreating. Fewer than half still pay for weight management, and most of those have folded it into diabetes, cardiac and sleep-apnoea codes. Access is now sorted by diagnosis. If your chart says type 2 diabetes or a prior heart attack, a pen arrives for a copay. If it says only obesity, you are in the cash tier. Prices there were supposed to keep sliding toward $245. Instead they have sat at $299 to $349 a month for injectables, and $149 to $299 for pills, since the manufacturers paused the step-down in mid-2027, citing demand and capacity. Medicare beneficiaries, under the Part D demonstration that took over from the 2026 bridge, are the cheapest customers in the country.

The growth came anyway: through pills bought on subscription, through Medicare, and through people who simply kept paying. It also came from a channel nobody planned for. Telehealth firms sell low-dose oral plans branded as quiet, promising calm, focus and freedom from craving, and they now count well over a million subscribers, many of them without obesity. No regulator has approved the drugs for anything like this; the alcohol trials are still in phase 3. The effect patients described in 2026 as feeling flat is now, in certain offices, described as being steady.

Washington pulls in two directions. The FDA cleared Lilly's retatrutide in December 2027 under a priority voucher, so a weekly pen now delivers close to 30 percent mean weight loss, the range that used to require surgery. Lilly rations it by supply and by a list price near $1,399, and bariatric surgeons report their first real dip in referrals. At the same time the agency, the FTC and a dozen state legislatures have closed doors. Broadcast and influencer advertising for these drugs is effectively over. Telehealth starts require a live visit and a documented BMI, and compounding is finished. Eleven states bar prescribing under twelve and require a specialist for teenagers. The restrictions bite hardest on the cash tier; the coded tier barely notices.

Mail fills the gap. Generic semaglutide costs under $50 a month in India and about a hundred Canadian dollars in Toronto, and Chinese manufacturers came online in 2027. Pens arrive in padded envelopes, and so-called research retatrutide is sold by the vial. Perhaps three million Americans use some unapproved supply.

The body has changed meaning. When thinness costs $149 a month, it stops saying much about anyone. A narrow waist now reads as medicated. What reads as expensive is muscle, which takes trainers, protein and time, and appetite, the visible pleasure of finishing a full plate. Unmedicated has become a boast on dating profiles and in casting calls. Wellness influencers, strength coaches and populist commentators use it with equal fervour, and plenty of the people photographed lifting are on a pen too. Gyms spent 2026 selling muscle preservation; now they sell muscle as display, and they are growing.

Food companies have stopped fighting. Snack and confectionery volumes keep easing and protein keeps climbing. Marketing is split between portion-tiered products for medicated households and frank indulgence for people who want to be seen hungry. Alcohol is still shrinking. Restaurants serve half plates at one table and tasting menus to performative eaters at the next.

Underneath, the population keeps cycling. Nearly half of those who have ever used the drugs have stopped and restarted at least once, usually when coverage, cash or patience ran out. Teenagers who started at thirteen are now fifteen. Nobody has data on either group beyond about six years. The ledger of known harms has not grown, which is reassuring or not depending on how long you think it takes to look.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renata Pruitt sets two alarms, one for work and one for Sunday's pill. It's Thursday. She checks the pharmacy app anyway. Refill: $299. She closes it.

At the hospital scheduling desk in Dayton, the new hire, Kyle, has a sticker on his water bottle, a small grey circle with the word quiet in lowercase. He doesn't snack. He doesn't look up when the phone lines stack. In the huddle the supervisor called him unflappable.

Lunch is in the break room. Marisol is on retatrutide through her husband's union plan. She eats four almonds and a protein yogurt and talks about her son's tuxedo fitting. Renata has the leftover lasagna and eats all of it. Nobody says anything. She notices that nobody says anything.

At three her daughter texts from school: a screenshot of a girl from her class, lifting, captioned natty, never pinned. Then: can we go to the specialist or not. Renata types we'll talk, deletes it, and types we'll talk.

Her sister in Toronto calls on the drive home. She's switched to the generic, ninety-four dollars. I could mail you some. Don't mail me anything.

Dinner. Darnell's pen lives in the butter compartment, because his A1c makes him a covered person. He used to have two beers on Thursdays. Now he has seltzer, asks how her day was, and listens carefully, the way he listens now.

After he's asleep she opens the app again. $299. The gym across from the Kroger has a banner: EAT. LIFT. FEEL IT. She thinks about the lasagna, how good it was, how hungry she's been all week. She doesn't hit refill. Not tonight.

rationale.badness: Median wellbeing is mixed: obesity falls from 36.4% to about 33.5%, and no new safety signal appears, so flourishing and public_health sit around 4.5. The harder losses are structural. Access is sorted by diagnosis code ("Diagnosis codes get a copay, obesity alone gets a stalled cash price or a mailed foreign generic"), about 3M users take unapproved product, and 46% of ever-users cycle with no long-horizon data. Inequality is highest (6.0) because the bottom third has the highest obesity, the least coverage and the most gray-market use. Epistemic is also 6.0: calm is marketed as 'quiet' while the same effect is logged as an unquantified side effect that no trial measures, and nobody can tell relief from loss. Autonomy is 5.5 for workplace pressure (managers praising 'unflappable' staff), price-driven stop-and-start, and gray-market dependence. Cohesion is 5.0 for mismatched appetites in couples, performative eating and the unresolved teen cohort. This is a recognisably harder society with new losers, not a refusal-grade one.
rationale.plausibility: It honours every stipulated driver: adoption +7.1pp to 18.1%, a stalled price at $299–349, employer retreat to 44%, no new indications, no safety signal, a ~29–30% triple agonist, no market shock, aesthetic inversion, restriction, and marketed personality. Mechanisms are mostly visible, such as the capacity-for-onshoring trade, coding audits and Chinese generics. The stretches are these. (1) Ever-used goes from 15% to 28% and current use from 11% to 18% in two years, which is steep and rests on a 'quiet' tier of only 1.2M, about 0.5% of adults. (2) Bottom-third use at 12%, with Medicaid in about 16 states, does not clearly account for the growth. (3) The 'unmedicated' muscle-over-thin inversion arrives fast, and Gallup's 'muscular' over 'thin' finding is asserted rather than derived. (4) Retatrutide is approved Dec 2027 with phase 3 filing planned for Q1 2027, which is very fast, though a priority voucher helps. (5) The new restriction regime is arguably bolted on, and reported pediatric use falling by two-thirds in under-12s looks tidy. (6) The 2026 pipeline notes put AUD phase 2 readouts in 2026, so 'phase 3 readouts 2029' is plausible but not derived. The summed generous assumptions land at about 5.
rationale.generativity: The world is rich in implied scenes. The prose has named characters and concrete objects: Renata and the $299 refill, Kyle's grey 'quiet' sticker, Marisol's four almonds, Darnell's pen in the butter compartment, and the 'natty' screenshot from the daughter. Scenes of eating as signal, a Toronto sister offering mail-order generics, and the gym banner 'EAT. LIFT. FEEL IT.' are all filmable. The fields supply further hooks: dating-profile 'on reta', musicians lowering their dose before tours, couples timing dose reductions around holidays, and diagnosis-coded household splits. The day-in-the-life shows rather than explains.

least_plausible_claims.quote: 46% of ever-users have stopped and restarted at least once
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: the figures do not reconcile. With 28% ever-users, ~10% currently off and 18.1% on, 46% cyclers plus the 10% still off means about 82% of ever-users have stopped at some point. That contradicts 38% one-year persistence and the large pool of recent starters.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Under-12 off-label prescribing fell by about two-thirds after 11 states barred it.
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude: the events place the 11-state bans around mid-2028, so a measured two-thirds drop by year-end is too fast. Few legislatures would have enacted, implemented and shown an effect that quickly.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Marisol is on retatrutide through her husband's union plan.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: the world says retatrutide launched in Feb 2028, is supply-allocated at about $1,399 list, and is outside Medicare and Medicaid obesity coverage. It also says employers have narrowed coverage to coded diagnoses. A union plan covering it for a non-coded user within months is unshown and convenient.

rationale.badness: The world is recognisably harder than 2026, though not catastrophic. Access is split by diagnosis code versus cash (employer coverage at 44%, 'coding drift' audits, Medicaid in ~16 states). A gray market of 3M users carries dosing and contamination harm. 'Quiet' plans sell reward blunting as a product with no RCT, which gives a real epistemic problem. Family and couple mismatches and the unstudied cycling and teen cohorts add cohesion and public-health cost, but the ledger is stipulated flat and no mass harm is shown.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver is visible in fields and events. Adoption reaches 18.1%, the price stalls at $299–349, employer coverage falls to 44%, retatrutide gives ~29%, the aesthetic inversion appears and 'quiet' is marketed. The indications list stays empty and the safety ledger shows no new signal. Nothing contradicts a driver. mechanism: The chains for price, coverage, gray market and culture are shown. The cycling figure (46% of ever-users) does not reconcile with 28% ever, ~10% off and 38% persistence. Marisol's union-plan retatrutide conflicts with the stated coverage limits, and a pill taken 'Sunday' clashes with daily orals. magnitude: Several figures sit at the aggressive edge. These include a 2.9pp fall in obesity, 28% ever-use, a two-thirds drop in under-12 prescribing and 11 state bans by mid-2028. A Dec 2027 retatrutide approval and a cultural inversion measured by Gallup within two years are also fast but defensible.
rationale.generativity: The prose gives a full ensemble: Renata with the refill app and the lasagna, Kyle with the 'quiet' sticker, Marisol with her four almonds, Darnell with his pen in the butter compartment, and the daughter's text about the specialist. The world fields add banners, dating-profile markers, dose timing around tours and holidays, and a Toronto sister mailing generics. It shows more than it explains, with a clear small-scale tension about whether to hit refill.
